(* The integer types' checked getters asZZ32, asZZ64, asNN32, asNN64 and asZZ answer at their edges and raise IntegerOverflow one past them, bitsAs keeps the bits, and the low-bits names answer on every type that declares them. *)
component IntegerConversionsWalk
export Executable

shown(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    IntLiteral => v.asString || " : IntLiteral"
    ZZ32 => v.asString || " : ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => v.asString || " : ZZ64"
    NN32 => v.asString || " : NN32"
    NN64 => v.asString || " : NN64"
    ZZ => v.asString || " : ZZ"
    else => v.asString || " : another type"
  end

raises(f: () -> Any): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(f())
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

run(): () = do
  (* ZZ32 values *)
  aMin: ZZ32 = -2147483647 - 1
  aMax: ZZ32 = 2147483647
  aZero: ZZ32 = 0
  aMOne: ZZ32 = -1
  (* ZZ64 values *)
  bMin: ZZ64 = -9223372036854775807 - 1
  bMax: ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807
  bZero: ZZ64 = 0
  bMOne: ZZ64 = -1
  b31: ZZ64 = 2147483648
  b31m: ZZ64 = 2147483647
  bN31: ZZ64 = -2147483648
  bN31m: ZZ64 = -2147483649
  b32: ZZ64 = 4294967296
  b32m: ZZ64 = 4294967295
  (* NN32 values *)
  cZero = unsigned(aZero)
  c31m = unsigned(aMax)
  c31 = unsigned(aMin)
  cMax = unsigned(aMOne)
  (* NN64 values *)
  dZero = unsigned(bZero)
  d31m = unsigned(b31m)
  d31 = unsigned(b31)
  d32m = unsigned(b32m)
  d32 = unsigned(b32)
  d63m = unsigned(bMax)
  d63 = unsigned(bMin)
  dMax = unsigned(bMOne)
  (* ZZ values *)
  eZero: ZZ = 0
  eMOne: ZZ = -1
  eN31: ZZ = -2147483648
  eN31m: ZZ = -2147483649
  e31m: ZZ = 2147483647
  e31: ZZ = 2147483648
  e32m: ZZ = 4294967295
  e32: ZZ = 4294967296
  eN63: ZZ = -9223372036854775808
  eN63m: ZZ = -9223372036854775809
  e63m: ZZ = 9223372036854775807
  e63: ZZ = 9223372036854775808
  e64m: ZZ = 18446744073709551615
  e64: ZZ = 18446744073709551616
  e32p5: ZZ = 4294967301
  e64p5: ZZ = 18446744073709551621

  (* ZZ32's five: asZZ32 is the identity, asZZ64 and asZZ equal the coercions, asNN32 and asNN64 raise below 0 *)
  assert(shown(aMin.asZZ32), "-2147483648 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ32 -2^31 is itself")
  assert(shown(aMax.asZZ32), "2147483647 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ32 2^31-1 is itself")
  assert(shown(aMin.asZZ64), "-2147483648 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the ZZ32 -2^31")
  assert(shown(aMax.asZZ64), "2147483647 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the ZZ32 2^31-1")
  assert(shown(aZero.asNN32), "0 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ32 0")
  assert(shown(aMax.asNN32), "2147483647 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ32 2^31-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => aMOne.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ32 -1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => aMin.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ32 -2^31 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(aZero.asNN64), "0 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ32 0")
  assert(shown(aMax.asNN64), "2147483647 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ32 2^31-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => aMOne.asNN64), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ32 -1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(aMin.asZZ), "-2147483648 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the ZZ32 -2^31")
  assert(shown(aMax.asZZ), "2147483647 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the ZZ32 2^31-1")

  (* ZZ64's five *)
  assert(shown(bN31.asZZ32), "-2147483648 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ64 -2^31")
  assert(shown(b31m.asZZ32), "2147483647 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ64 2^31-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => bN31m.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ64 -2^31-1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => b31.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ64 2^31 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => bMin.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ64 -2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(bMin.asZZ64), "-9223372036854775808 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the ZZ64 -2^63 is itself")
  assert(shown(bMax.asZZ64), "9223372036854775807 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the ZZ64 2^63-1 is itself")
  assert(shown(bZero.asNN32), "0 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 0")
  assert(shown(b31.asNN32), "2147483648 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 2^31")
  assert(shown(b32m.asNN32), "4294967295 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 2^32-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => bMOne.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 -1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => b32.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 2^32 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => bMin.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the ZZ64 -2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(bZero.asNN64), "0 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ64 0")
  assert(shown(bMax.asNN64), "9223372036854775807 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ64 2^63-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => bMOne.asNN64), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ64 -1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => bMin.asNN64), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the ZZ64 -2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(bMin.asZZ), "-9223372036854775808 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the ZZ64 -2^63")
  assert(shown(bMax.asZZ), "9223372036854775807 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the ZZ64 2^63-1")

  (* NN32's five, at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ *)
  assert(shown(cZero.asZZ32), "0 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN32 0")
  assert(shown(c31m.asZZ32), "2147483647 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN32 2^31-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => c31.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN32 2^31 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => cMax.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN32 2^32-1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(c31.asZZ64), "2147483648 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN32 2^31")
  assert(shown(cMax.asZZ64), "4294967295 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN32 2^32-1")
  assert(shown(cZero.asNN32), "0 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN32 0 is itself")
  assert(shown(cMax.asNN32), "4294967295 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN32 2^32-1 is itself")
  assert(shown(c31.asNN64), "2147483648 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the NN32 2^31")
  assert(shown(cMax.asNN64), "4294967295 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the NN32 2^32-1")
  assert(shown(c31.asZZ), "2147483648 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the NN32 2^31")
  assert(shown(cMax.asZZ), "4294967295 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the NN32 2^32-1")

  (* NN64's five, at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ *)
  assert(shown(dZero.asZZ32), "0 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN64 0")
  assert(shown(d31m.asZZ32), "2147483647 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN64 2^31-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => d31.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN64 2^31 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => d63.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN64 2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => dMax.asZZ32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the NN64 2^64-1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(dZero.asZZ64), "0 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN64 0")
  assert(shown(d63m.asZZ64), "9223372036854775807 : ZZ64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN64 2^63-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => d63.asZZ64), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN64 2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => dMax.asZZ64), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ64 of the NN64 2^64-1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(dZero.asNN32), "0 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 0")
  assert(shown(d31.asNN32), "2147483648 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 2^31")
  assert(shown(d32m.asNN32), "4294967295 : NN32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 2^32-1")
  assert(raises(fn () => d32.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 2^32 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => d63.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 2^63 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(raises(fn () => dMax.asNN32), "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN32 of the NN64 2^64-1 throws IntegerOverflow")
  assert(shown(d63.asNN64), "9223372036854775808 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the NN64 2^63 is itself")
  assert(shown(dMax.asNN64), "18446744073709551615 : NN64", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asNN64 of the NN64 2^64-1 is itself")
  assert(shown(d63.asZZ), "9223372036854775808 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the NN64 2^63")
  assert(shown(dMax.asZZ), "18446744073709551615 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ of the NN64 2^64-1")

  (* ZZ's five *)
  assert(shown(eN31.asZZ32), "-2147483648 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ -2^31")
  assert(shown(e31m.asZZ32), "2147483647 : ZZ32", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": asZZ32 of the ZZ 2^31-1")

(* The object IntLiteral's conversions, strings, equality and order answer at its value 0, and ZZ32's big answers at the ends of ZZ32. *)
component IntLiteralTextWalk
export Executable

shown(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    IntLiteral => v.asString || " : IntLiteral"
    ZZ32 => v.asString || " : ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => v.asString || " : ZZ64"
    NN32 => v.asString || " : NN32"
    NN64 => v.asString || " : NN64"
    ZZ => v.asString || " : ZZ"
    else => v.asString || " : another type"
  end

run(): () = do
    x = IntLiteral
    assert(shown(x.asZZ32), "0 : ZZ32", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\": the object IntLiteral as a ZZ32 is 0")
    assert(shown(x.asZZ64), "0 : ZZ64", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\": the object IntLiteral as a ZZ64 is 0")
    assert(shown(x.asNN32), "0 : NN32", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\": the object IntLiteral as an NN32 is 0")
    assert(shown(x.asNN64), "0 : NN64", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\": the object IntLiteral as an NN64 is 0")
    assert(shown(x.asZZ), "0 : ZZ", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\": the object IntLiteral as a ZZ is 0")
    assert(x.asString, "0", "pins the library: the object IntLiteral's asString is 0")
    assert(x.asExprString, "0", "pins the library: the object IntLiteral's asExprString is 0")
    assert(x = x, "pins the library: the object IntLiteral equals itself")
    assert(NOT (x < x), "pins the library: the object IntLiteral is not less than itself")
    assert(x <= x, "pins the library: the object IntLiteral is at most itself")
    assert(NOT (x > x), "pins the library: the object IntLiteral is not greater than itself")
    assert(x >= x, "pins the library: the object IntLiteral is at least itself")
    assert((x CMP x) = EqualTo, "pins the library: the object IntLiteral CMP itself is EqualTo")
    hi: ZZ32 = 2147483647
    lo: ZZ32 = -2147483647 - 1
    assert(shown(big(hi)), "2147483647 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": big of the ZZ32 2^31-1 is exact")
    assert(shown(big(lo)), "-2147483648 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": big of the ZZ32 -2^31 is exact")
    println "PASS"
  end

end
tests=IntegerConversionHelpersCompiled
link
run
run_out_contains=PASS
(* On the compiled path, the nativeHelpers that the integer types' checked getters name answer a value that the target type holds and raise IntegerOverflow on one that it does not, an NN32 carried in a ZZ32 and an NN64 in a ZZ64. *)
component IntegerConversionHelpersCompiled
export Executable

toZZ32(a:ZZ64):ZZ32 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.longOverflowingToInt")
toNN32(a:ZZ64):ZZ32 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleUnsignedIntArith.longOverflowingToUnsignedInt")
toZZ64(a:ZZ):ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong")
toNN64(a:ZZ):ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToUnsignedLong")
big64(a:ZZ64):ZZ = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.makeZZfromZZ64")
sub64(a:ZZ64, b:ZZ64):ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleLongArith.longOverflowingSub")
addZ(a:ZZ, b:ZZ):ZZ = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.add")
subZ(a:ZZ, b:ZZ):ZZ = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.sub")
negZ(a:ZZ):ZZ = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.neg")

overflows32(f: () -> ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore f()
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
    Exception => false
  end

overflows64(f: () -> ZZ64): Boolean =
  try
    ignore f()
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
    Exception => false
  end

run():() = do
  s0: ZZ64 = 0
  s1: ZZ64 = 1
  m1: ZZ64 = -1
  mx: ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807
  mn: ZZ64 = sub64(-9223372036854775807, 1)
  h31m: ZZ64 = 2147483647
  h31: ZZ64 = 2147483648
  l31: ZZ64 = sub64(-2147483647, 1)
  l31m: ZZ64 = sub64(-2147483647, 2)
  h32m: ZZ64 = 4294967295
  h32: ZZ64 = 4294967296
  assert(toZZ32(h31m).asString, "2147483647", "ZZ64 2^31-1 to ZZ32")
  assert(toZZ32(l31).asString, "-2147483648", "ZZ64 -2^31 to ZZ32")
  assert(overflows32(fn () => toZZ32(h31)), "ZZ64 2^31 to ZZ32 overflows")
  assert(overflows32(fn () => toZZ32(l31m)), "ZZ64 -2^31-1 to ZZ32 overflows")
  assert(toNN32(s0).asString, "0", "ZZ64 or NN64 0 to NN32")
  assert(toNN32(h31).asString, "-2147483648", "ZZ64 or NN64 2^31 to NN32, the bits of the NN32 2^31")
  assert(toNN32(h32m).asString, "-1", "ZZ64 or NN64 2^32-1 to NN32, the bits of the NN32 2^32-1")
  assert(overflows32(fn () => toNN32(h32)), "ZZ64 or NN64 2^32 to NN32 overflows")
  assert(overflows32(fn () => toNN32(m1)), "ZZ64 -1, the NN64 2^64-1, to NN32 overflows")
  assert(overflows32(fn () => toNN32(mn)), "ZZ64 -2^63, the NN64 2^63, to NN32 overflows")
  z0: ZZ = big64(s0)
  z1: ZZ = big64(s1)
  zm1: ZZ = negZ(z1)
  z63m: ZZ = big64(mx)
  z63: ZZ = addZ(z63m, z1)
  zn63: ZZ = big64(mn)
  zn63m: ZZ = subZ(zn63, z1)
  z64: ZZ = 18446744073709551616
  z64m: ZZ = subZ(z64, z1)
  assert(toZZ64(z63m).asString, "9223372036854775807", "ZZ 2^63-1 to ZZ64")
  assert(toZZ64(zn63).asString, "-9223372036854775808", "ZZ -2^63 to ZZ64")
  assert(overflows64(fn () => toZZ64(z63)), "ZZ 2^63 to ZZ64 overflows")
  assert(overflows64(fn () => toZZ64(zn63m)), "ZZ -2^63-1 to ZZ64 overflows")
  assert(toNN64(z0).asString, "0", "ZZ 0 to NN64")
  assert(toNN64(z63).asString, "-9223372036854775808", "ZZ 2^63 to NN64, the bits of the NN64 2^63")
  assert(toNN64(z64m).asString, "-1", "ZZ 2^64-1 to NN64, the bits of the NN64 2^64-1")
  assert(overflows64(fn () => toNN64(z64)), "ZZ 2^64 to NN64 overflows")
  assert(overflows64(fn () => toNN64(zm1)), "ZZ -1 to NN64 overflows")
  println("PASS")
end

end

# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.

+unchanged, and it drops \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} from the sentence on \VAR{narrow}:
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} has neither \VAR{narrow} nor \VAR{widen}, and converts to a
+fixed-size type only by a getter.
+The passage gains one box, and the box of \secref{revival-shifts} beside it names
+the paragraph that now states \VAR{narrow}.
+The change of \secref{revival-shifts} no longer gives \VAR{narrow} on
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided on
+6~November 2026 that each integer type has getters that convert and throw
+\TYP{IntegerOverflow} where the value does not fit, that the fixed-size types
+have getters for the bit pattern, that \VAR{narrow}, \VAR{widen}, \VAR{signed},
+\VAR{unsigned} and \VAR{big} stay as the conversions that keep bits, declared on
+every type to which they apply, and that the \VAR{narrow} and \VAR{widen} of
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} go.
+The team's later compiler library declares the getter \VAR{asZZ32} of
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which throws \TYP{IntegerOverflow} for a value that does not
+fit, and the four getters \VAR{bitsAsNN32}, \VAR{bitsAsNN64}, \VAR{bitsAsZZ32}
+and \VAR{bitsAsZZ64} (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi},
+in the revival's repository); this working draft says in general that an
+integer result too large for its type throws \TYP{IntegerOverflow}; and a plain
+name that checks beside a name that says it keeps bits is the pattern of Swift
+and Julia.
+Before the revision \library\ declared each of the five methods on some of the
+integer types only, so that a call on another type went through a coercion to
+another type's method: \VAR{widen} of the \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} \EXP{2^{64}-1} gave
+the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} \EXP{-1}, and \VAR{unsigned} of an \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} gave
+an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}.
+The \VAR{narrow} and \VAR{widen} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} kept the low 32 and 64 bits,
+so that \VAR{widen}, under the name of a widening, narrowed, and turned
+\EXP{2^{63}} negative.
+A reversal would declare \VAR{narrow} and \VAR{widen} on \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} again,
+keeping the low bits, beside the getters or in their place, and would remove the
+methods that return their argument unchanged.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/integer-conversions-2026-11-06.md} in the
+revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] The interpreter computes each getter and each method as the text
+states, on all five types, and refuses \VAR{narrow} or \VAR{widen} of a value of
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} at the call, which finds no declaration.
+The compiled path, which until it is built on \library\ compiles against a
+smaller library of its own, declares of the getters only \VAR{asZZ32} of
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{asNN32} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
+\VAR{asNN64} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \VAR{asZZ} of the four fixed-size types and
+the four getters that keep the bits, none on \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}; and of the
+methods only \VAR{narrow} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64},
+\VAR{widen} of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \VAR{unsigned} of
+\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and \VAR{signed} of
+\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and of \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, with no \VAR{big} (row~349 of the
+revival's gap ledger).
+The getters are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/IntegerConversionsWalk.fss},
+and the helpers that five of them name by
+\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/IntegerConversionHelpersCompiled.fss}.
+No line of the revival's model program calls any of these conversions.
+\item[Original text] None: no chapter of this working draft names \VAR{asZZ32},
+\VAR{asZZ64}, \VAR{asNN32}, \VAR{asNN64}, \VAR{asZZ}, the four getters that keep
+the bits, \VAR{narrow}, \VAR{widen}, \VAR{signed}, \VAR{unsigned} or \VAR{big}.

+\end{description}

    getter max(): Just[\N\] = just (modulus-1)

    var state: N = seed MOD modulus

    reseed(seedvec:Indexed[\N,ZZ32\]): LinearCongruential[\N\] =
        do state := seedvec[0] MOD modulus; self end

    random(): N =
        do state := ((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus; state end

    perturbed(perturbvec:Generator[\ZZ32\]): LinearCongruential[\N\] = do

        newseed: N := state

    perturbed(perturbvec:Generator[\ZZ32\]): MersenneTwisterInit = do

        spacing = (gen.max.get - gen.min.get + 1) DIV |range|

    end

### 6.0 What every option shares

- **The compiled path until the switch-over.** No option adds a declaration to the prelude (P-37) or repairs its text (P-38). So until the switch-over the compiled path answers as Run C and Run Z show. After it, the compiled path runs the one library's members and helpers.
- **`ZZ`'s low-bits members need two helpers**, `x.intValue()` and `x.longValue()`, before the switch-over, in every option that keeps them (1 to 4, 7, 8). The record files them as class C, a new helper [3].
- **`ZZ32`'s `big`** moves onto `makeZZfromZZ32` under every option. It is exact and waits only on item 331's group (section 2.2).
- **A new binding over `NN32` or `NN64`** is tested on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ, 2^31 and up for `NN32` and 2^63 and up for `NN64` [4].
- **The six transfer helpers**, such as `makeZZ64FromNN64WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN64ArgumentType`, return their argument unchanged. `signed` and `unsigned` bind them, and the compiled path's rewrite also passes every value of an `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char` binding through them [4]. An option that makes `signed` or `unsigned` raise binds new helpers and leaves these six alone.
- **The model program**: no effect in any option (section 5).
- **Rows 858 and 859** close in every option that declares the names on every type (1, 2, 3, 4, 7). In option 6 they close too, except that `narrow` and `widen` of a `ZZ` are then refused on purpose: by reading, `ZZ` coerces into no type that declares them.

### Option 1. The low bits everywhere, with today's names declared on all five types

The evidence's way A [2].

- **The one library.** The 8 lossy members keep the low bits, as today. Nine members are added, each `= self` or a coercion, so that no call goes by coercion: `narrow` on `NN32`, `widen` on `NN64`, `big` on `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, `signed` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and `unsigned` on `NN32` and `NN64`. The 5 gaps stay compositions, with the order rule written down: change the width first, then the sign.
- **Results that change.** `widen` of an `NN64` gives the `NN64` itself, not the `ZZ64` -1. `unsigned` of an `NN32` gives the `NN32`, not an `NN64`. `narrow` of an `NN32` gives itself, not an "Ambiguous coercion". `big` of an `NN64` or a `ZZ` answers.
- **Helpers.** Only `ZZ`'s two (6.0).
- **The specification.** Sentences for `widen`, `big`, `signed` and `unsigned` beside `basic-integers.tex:39-45`, with an Appendix I entry.
- **Tests.** No test changes. New walk and compiled guards for the nine members and rows 858 and 859.
- **Size.** One rung [1] [2].
- **What it leaves.** Item 20: the low 64 bits, P-72 extended to `ZZ`. Item 338: the low bits. PLAN.md:73: no checked form; at the switch-over the three compiled tests of section 2.5 are respelled, two of them Steele's.

content.content:
- F-124 **On the compiled path, at or beyond the width of `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, `LSHIFT` gives 0 and `RSHIFT` the sign; both reverse on a negative count, and `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits.** "The sign" is 0 for a nonnegative value and -1 for a negative one. `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s `narrow` to 32 bits keeps the low 32 bits. `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` keep their own rules, and `asZZ32` throws out of range. Negation, absolute value and division overflow only at the minimum value and test exactly for it, so the minimum raises `IntegerOverflow`, and `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` answer 0. Addition and subtraction test the sign bits, and multiplication computes the exact product (`Math.multiplyExact` on `ZZ64`, a range-checked 64-bit product on `ZZ32`). So these raise `IntegerOverflow` on every overflow, and a zero factor answers 0. `ZZ`'s `<<<` raises a catchable `IntegerOverflow` on a shift that it cannot represent (row 386). Gated by `compiler_tests/IntSemanticsRungB.fss`, and for addition and subtraction by the team's `library_tests/Integer3.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-compiled/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-132 **Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit, as the specification says.** It builds P-73. Every arithmetic operation on a fixed width whose result can leave its type raises it, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included, and a program can catch it. Three kinds of operation raise nothing: the wrapping operators (F-130) and `narrow`, the written conversion of a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` or an `NN64` to `NN32` (P-72), which keep the low bits; and the shifts `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, which lose the bits shifted out (F-125). Gated by `tests/FixedWidthOverflowRungB.fss` (`+`, `-`, `DOT` (`·`), `DIV`, negation and absolute value, on the four fixed widths) and `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` (`^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM`). The compiled path is outside this fact. Its known gaps: the compiler prelude's ranges raise `IntegerOverflow` where their bounds sum beyond `ZZ32` (row 453); and `^` saturates, throws an uncatchable Java exception or adds (rows 523 to 525). Its `CHOOSE` raises `IntegerOverflow` as walk's does (F-305). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overflow-natives/REPORT.md` section 13; `compile-ladder/rung-size-range/REPORT.md` section 12.
- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits; a value that does not fit wraps, and nothing is thrown. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-62` (`narrow` and the shifts) and `:530-542` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
18:- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
30:- F-32 **The compiled path cannot reuse walk's glue classes, the Java classes that 102 of the one library's 443 live native bindings still name.** A native binding is a library body `builtinPrimitive("…")`; its string names a glue class, which takes walk's boxed values, or a static helper of `nativeHelpers/`, over plain Java values, which both paths call (F-298; F-299 holds the 341 that name one). Matched against those helpers at `a1f8c4b8b`, before any binding moved, the 449 were: 154 whose operation the compiler's prelude already binds to a helper at the same owner and signature, so only the binding's string changes, to name that helper (P-58); 59 whose helper exists, but no binding names it under that name and signature, 23 of them under a name that the compiler's prelude gives to another helper, such as the 12 wrapping operators (row 348); 158 that need a new helper; and 78 that need more, 36 methods of native I/O objects and 42 with no compiled analogue. Of the 449, 29 are object `IntLiteral`'s (`FortressBuiltin.fss:486-563`), 4 among the 154 and 25 among the 158; none of them can move yet, since their helpers take and answer the compiled path's `IntLiteral`, which walk's values cannot be, and walk reaches no `IntLiteral` native while its numeral is an `Int` (P-76; row 578). `println` writes through `stdOut`, a plain Fortress `Writer` over `JavaBufferedWriter`, whose natives name `fileOps` helpers (F-330). MicroGPT's `nanoTime` names a helper (F-314); it also needs `getProgramArgsPrim`, which `System` calls as it loads (P-170 replaces it); and `NativeArray`. The last two have no compiled analogue. The 42 with no analogue: `NativeArray`'s 7 move onto a compiled store before array decision A (P-169), and `Thread`, `Reflect` and `printTaskTrace` are off microGPT's path. Detail: `compile-ladder/climb-batch-27/RECORD.md`, "The count of the bindings"; `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 2; `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-23.md`, section 4, "The planner's probes", "On the new base" and "The count".

\newpage
\section{Integers}
\seclabel{basic-integers}

The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) encompasses all finite integers,
the results of starting from \EXP{0} and repeatedly adding or subtracting \EXP{1} a finite number of times.

\Library\ also declare four integer types of fixed size.
The five integer types are these:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) is the set of integers (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (\STR{ZZ64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit two's-complement form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\STR{ZZ32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit two's-complement form.
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} (\STR{NN64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit unsigned binary form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\STR{NN32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit unsigned binary form.
\end{tabbing}

Like every number type, each of them is a subtype of \TYP{Number} and of no other
number type (\secref{basic-rationals}), and each coerces into \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

(* deal with negative numbers because negating the most negative number
 * that n-bits can represent in twos-complement becomes the same negative number.
 * With 8 bits we would have -128 = 0xff. Negating -128 is
 * -128 ^ 0xff + 1 = 127 + 1 = -128
 *)
radixHelper(base:ZZ64,val:ZZ64):String = do
    n = (|/(val / base)\|).asZZ64
    if n =/= 0 then
        radixHelper(base, n) radixConvert(-narrow(val REM base))
    else
        radixConvert(-narrow(val REM base))
    end
end

radix(base:ZZ64,val:ZZ64):String = do
    if val < 0 then
        "-" radixHelper(base,val)

content.content:
### 3.2 The library as the team wrote it

`git blame` on today's lines stops at a parentless snapshot of 2012 (`^5a68404fd`), because the conversion of the history cut its parent links. That snapshot's author field names no one who wrote these lines [7]. The authors below are the evidence's reconstruction, which searched the earlier history and the snapshots [8]. The lines of the revival are those that `git blame` gives to "Claude" [1].

- **`ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, `narrow`.** Present in the record's first commit, `72ae6881b` (2007-01-04, the account `jm143038`, Jan-Willem Maessen). It was bound to `Int$FromLong`, which called `Int.rc`, and `Int.rc` threw "Overflow of ZZ32" [9]. It stayed checked, with an error that ends the run, to the team's last commit `a874948ac`. The revival made the error catchable (`413f36ac0`, row 347), and then made it keep the low 32 bits (`d6faad28f`, 2026-09-24), by P-72 [8].
- **`NN64` to `NN32`, `narrow`; `NN32`'s `widen`; `signed` and `unsigned`.** Guy Steele, `dc41d5000` (2008-07-21, his first commit, which added `NN32`, `NN64` and `QQ`). They keep the low bits or the bits. His test asserts the low 32 bits of 2^64 - 1 and 2^63 (`ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:210-211`) and that `signed` of 2^64 - 1 is below `signed` of 0 (`:219`) [8].
- **`ZZ32`'s `widen`.** In the first commit. Maessen's doc comment of 2008: "widen converts a ZZ32 into a valid ZZ64 quantity." [10]
- **`ZZ64`'s `big`.** Christine Flood, `25acd32f7` (2008-07-10) [8].
- **`ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen`.** The account Crink, `e1567d62f` (2009-09-10): "Added methods to ZZ to convert to ZZ32 or ZZ64. The nomenclature needs work, in my opinion. Incidentally, my first ever use of Java." Reverted the same day (`02e648434`) and put back the next day (`8d2eb48f5`), unchanged to `a874948ac`, with the comment at fss:1082 [8] [11]. The history records no review. The record leaves open whose account Crink is: "likely external SCA contributor" (`research/authorship.md:68`) [10].
- **`ZZ32`'s `narrow` and `big`, `ZZ64`'s `widen`, and every coercion between integer types**: the revival, `d846e3644` (2026-09-27), when the types became siblings. Before it, `ZZ32` lay under `ZZ64` under `ZZ` and needed no coercion [8].

So at the team's last commit, walk's library was mixed [12]:

- The signed narrowing, `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, raised.
- The unsigned narrowing and `ZZ`'s two kept the low bits.
- The changes of sign kept the bits.

content.content:
them, and \VAR{narrow} no longer converts a value of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.}

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.
\revision{revival-shifts}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither
\VAR{narrow} nor \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT}, which \library\ declare on the
integer types; the paragraph above states the rules the revival decided for the
shifts, and the paragraph on the methods that keep bits, before it, the rule for
\VAR{narrow} (\secref{revival-int-conversions}).}

subtype of two different instantiations of one parameterized trait, which
the compiled type checker enforces for type arguments and numerals, with the exceptions \appref{spec-changes} names, and this draft had
not stated, and
rewrites the examples that the rule refuses.

\appref{spec-changes} lists every change with its reason, the original
text, and the alternative not taken.

content.content:
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the decision names the integer numerals too.
The conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though exact, stays explicit, since
that decision names only \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the numerals.
The examples of this paragraph convert numerals and are unchanged.
\Library\ give an integer numeral the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, from which
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} coerces, and the compiled type checker types a numeral so
(\secref{literals}, \secref{revival-numeral-type}).
The interpreter does not yet: it gives an integer numeral outside the range of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} a wider integer type, and so does not yet convert it.
The compiled path's own library declares no coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
from an integer type or an integer numeral; there \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and integer
numerals convert to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} only explicitly, and the other integer types not at all.}

content.content:
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
